details:
**Nicolae Ceaușescu and Elena**
The Communist dictator of Romania from 1965 to 1989, who ruled from Bucharest. During the 1989 Romanian Revolution, he and his wife Elena were tried by a hasty military tribunal and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day; the footage was shown on television. The near-universal giveaway for Romania.

**Securitate**
Communist Romania's secret police, founded in 1948 under Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and greatly expanded under Ceaușescu. Its former deputy chief Ion Mihai Pacepa defected and wrote the memoir Red Horizons. It was rumored to give dissidents cancer with radiation (the "Radu gun"), and it was replaced after 1989 by the SRI (Romanian Intelligence Service).

**Decree 770**
Ceaușescu's 1966 decree that banned most abortions and restricted contraception in order to boost the birth rate. Women with many children were honored as "heroine mothers." The policy led to a surge of unwanted children placed in notoriously overcrowded orphanages.

**July Theses**
A 1971 speech by Ceaușescu, given after a visit to China and North Korea, that launched a "mini cultural revolution." It reimposed strict ideological control over culture and built up a personality cult in imitation of Kim Il-sung's regime.

**Timișoara and László Tőkés**
The 1989 revolution began in the western city of Timișoara when the authorities tried to evict László Tőkés, an ethnic Hungarian Reformed pastor who had criticized the regime, including its "systematization" policy. Protests in his defense were bloodily repressed, and Ceaușescu's final public speech in Bucharest was drowned out by crowds chanting "Timișoara."

**Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and the Grivița strike**
Romania's first Communist leader (1947–1965), who as a young railway worker helped lead the 1933 Grivița railroad strike and was sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. He led the Party's "prison faction" and purged the Moscow faction of Ana Pauker, a Communist leader who became the world's first female foreign minister. Forced labor under his regime was used to dig the Danube–Black Sea Canal.

**Iron Guard**
Romania's interwar fascist, antisemitic movement, also called the Legion of the Archangel Michael, whose death squads included the Nicadori. Under Horia Sima it shared power with Ion Antonescu in the "National Legionary State" (1940–1941) before Antonescu crushed it during the Legionnaires' Rebellion of January 1941.

**Ion Antonescu**
The pro-Nazi military dictator, styled Conducător ("Leader"), who ruled Romania for most of World War II after forcing King Carol II to abdicate in 1940. He joined Operation Barbarossa to retake Bessarabia, which had been ceded to the Soviet Union. He was overthrown in King Michael I's coup of August 1944, which switched Romania to the Allied side.

**Ploiești and Operation Tidal Wave**
Ploiești was the center of Romania's oil industry and one of the Axis's most important fuel sources. In Operation Tidal Wave (1943), US bombers made a costly low-level raid on its refineries.

**Systematization and the Palace of the People**
Ceaușescu's urban-planning program, inspired by North Korea, which demolished historic neighborhoods and villages to build uniform apartment blocks and huge "hunger circus" food halls. Its centerpiece was the enormous Palace of the People (House of the People) in Bucharest.

**Petru Groza and the abdication of King Michael I**
Petru Groza headed the Soviet-backed government installed in 1945, which crushed the democratic opposition led by Iuliu Maniu of the National Peasant Party. In 1947 King Michael I, the last king of Romania's Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty, was forced to abdicate, and Romania became a People's Republic.

**Carol II and Magda Lupescu**
The interwar king whose relationship with his mistress Magda Lupescu scandalized the country. He returned to take the throne in 1930, feuded with the National Peasant Party, set up a royal dictatorship with the Străjeria youth organization, and relied on a weak line of fortifications nicknamed the "Imaginot Line." He was forced to abdicate in 1940.

**National Salvation Front**
The organization, led by former Communists such as Ion Iliescu, that took power after Ceaușescu fell in 1989. Its rule prompted the Golaniad protests in Bucharest's University Square and the violent Mineriads, in which miners were brought to the capital to attack protesters.

**World War I and Greater Romania**
Romania entered World War I on the Allied side in 1916 after two years of neutrality, was quickly defeated, and left the war with the Armistice of Focșani. Queen Marie lobbied at the Paris Peace Conference, and Romania gained Transylvania, Bukovina, and Bessarabia, roughly doubling its territory. In 1919 its army occupied Budapest, ending Béla Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic.

**Dacia, Wallachia, and Vlad the Impaler**
In antiquity the region was Dacia, whose king Decebalus was defeated by the Roman emperor Trajan at Sarmizegetusa. Its medieval principalities, Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania, were home to Vlad III the Impaler, Stephen the Great, and John Hunyadi, and were briefly united by Michael the Brave in 1600. Romania won full independence from the Ottomans after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, under Carol I.
